925.title: Tulsidas (the Ramcharitmanas opening and the Hanuman Chalisa, verse by verse)
925.hook: Tulsidas (the Ramcharitmanas opening and the Hanuman Chalisa, verse by verse)
925.tomorrow: Tulsidas (the Ramcharitmanas opening and the Hanuman Chalisa, verse by verse)
925.howItsDone: Readers of the Ramcharitmanas begin with its opening invocations, and the line about the whole world being full of Sita and Ram is often recited on its own with folded hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tulsidas bowed to Vani and Vinayaka at the door of the Ramcharitmanas, and wrote for his own heart's joy.

Speeches at a wedding usually go the same way. Thank the parents. Thank the friends who flew in. Thank the cooks. Then, if the speaker is brave, a joke about the uncle who argues with everyone. Tulsidas, at the door of his great poem, does something like that, but stranger. He bows to his teacher. He bows to the saints. And then, with what sounds like a straight face, he bows to the wicked, the people who wish others harm. He means it. And the reason he gives is the lesson.
screen: `HE BOWS TO THE TEACHER.` → `HE BOWS TO THE SAINTS.` → `THEN HE BOWS TO THE WICKED.`

segments.voice: The opening of the Ramcharitmanas is a long series of bows. First the teacher. Then the saints, and here Tulsidas has a lovely picture. He calls the company of good people a pilgrimage that walks: like Prayag, which the poem calls the king of pilgrimage places, but moving about the world on its own feet. You don't travel to it. It comes down your street. Then he bows to the wicked, sincerely, he says: people glad at another's loss and sad at another's gain. Why bow to them? He doesn't pretend they're good. Part of it is a poet's humility: he asks even the hostile reader to be kind to the poem. The deeper reason is a picture of the world. Tulsidas says the maker made this world a mixture, the living and the lifeless, good qualities and faults, all woven together. And the saint is like the swan in the old story, that can take the milk out of milk mixed with water, and leave the water behind. The world isn't sorted in advance. Good and bad come mixed, sometimes inside the same person. The work is to take the milk. Then the bow gets wider still. Knowing the whole world to be full of Sita and Ram, Tulsidas says, he bows to it all with joined palms. Not saints on one side and the wicked on the other, but a whole mixed world, greeted with folded hands before the story even starts.
screen: `A PILGRIMAGE THAT WALKS.` · `A BOW TO THE WICKED.` · `THE SWAN TAKES THE MILK.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE WORLD FULL OF SITA AND RAM.`

segments.voice: Bring your palms together at your chest, or just rest your hands, and bring to mind three people: someone good to you, someone you hardly notice, someone you find difficult. For each, without changing your opinion, look for the milk in the mixture, one small good thing that's really there. Let a quiet bow go toward each of them, and if you pray, hold all three before God.
Tulsidas. The poet who, at the door of the Ramcharitmanas, bowed to the saints, to the wicked, and to the whole world as full of Sita and Ram.
Your line: the swan takes the milk. Good and bad come mixed, and the milk is still there to find. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 925 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TULSIDAS (THE RAMCHARITMANAS OPENING AND THE HANUMAN CHALISA, VERSE BY VERSE).`

926.title: Tulsidas (the Ramcharitmanas opening and the Hanuman Chalisa, verse by verse)
926.hook: Tulsidas (the Ramcharitmanas opening and the Hanuman Chalisa, verse by verse)
926.howItsDone: Devotees of Hanuman recite the Hanuman Chalisa, often from memory, at home and in temples, and some make a point of saying it on Tuesdays and Saturdays.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tulsidas bowed to the saints, to the wicked, and to the whole world as full of Sita and Ram. The swan takes the milk.

A truck driver in traffic, murmuring under his breath. A student outside an exam hall, lips moving. A grandmother on a Tuesday evening, a small book open on her lap that she doesn't need, because she knows every word. They could all be saying the same thing: a hymn to Hanuman, short enough to say in a few minutes, steady enough to lean on. Tradition gives it to Tulsidas, and the hymn signs his name near its end.
screen: `MURMURED IN TRAFFIC.` → `KNOWN BY HEART.` → `THE HANUMAN CHALISA.`

segments.voice: The Hanuman Chalisa doesn't start with Hanuman. It starts with a mirror. The first couplet says, roughly: with the dust from my teacher's lotus feet I polish the mirror of my mind, and then I sing the pure fame of Ram. Before praising anyone, clean the glass, so what you see isn't smudged by you. The second couplet is even more honest. Knowing myself to be without understanding, it says, I remember Hanuman, son of the wind. Give me strength, wisdom and knowledge, and take away my troubles. That's the posture of the whole hymn. Not I am strong, but I'm not wise enough, so I'm calling on the one who is. Then the verses begin: victory to Hanuman, ocean of knowledge and virtue. They praise him piece by piece: his strength, his speed, his leap across the sea, the healing herb that revived Lakshman. But one line says what all that strength is for. Hanuman is the guard at Ram's door. All that power, used for service, near Ram, doing what's needed. Near the end, the poet steps forward with his own name. Tulsidas, the hymn says, is forever Hari's servant, and he asks the Lord to make a home in his heart. So the man who once crossed a flooded river for his wife ends up describing himself the way he describes Hanuman: a servant, with a strength that stands at the door.
screen: `POLISH THE MIRROR OF THE MIND.` · `WITHOUT UNDERSTANDING, I REMEMBER.` · `THE GUARD AT RAM'S DOOR.` · then, large: `TULSIDAS, FOREVER HARI'S SERVANT.`

segments.voice: Picture your mind as a glass with the day's smudges on it, a worry, a grudge, a hurry, and with each breath out, let one smudge soften. Then, if it feels honest, admit one thing you don't understand right now, and ask quietly for the strength to serve anyway. If you pray, you can turn that asking to God, or to Hanuman, in whatever words you already use.
Tulsidas. The poet of Ram, to whom tradition gives the Hanuman Chalisa, the hymn that cleans the mirror of the mind and ends by calling Tulsidas forever Hari's servant.
Your line: polish the mirror. Clean the glass first, then sing. Day nine hundred twenty-six, done.

927.title: Surdas
927.hook: a singer by the river stops singing about himself
927.howItsDone: Songs from the Sursagar are sung in Krishna temples and homes in north India, and in the Pushti Marg tradition founded by Vallabhacharya they are part of the daily service before Krishna's image.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tulsidas and the Hanuman Chalisa, which polishes the mirror of the mind and ends with the poet as Hari's servant.

A singer sits near a river and sings about himself. How low he has fallen. How far he is from God. How little he deserves. The songs are lovely, and they are sad. That's how one old account remembers Surdas before his life turned. Tradition says he was blind, and lived beside the Yamuna, in the country of Braj, where Krishna grew up. One day a teacher named Vallabhacharya stops to listen. He hears the sad songs through. Then he says one thing, and it changes what Surdas sings from then on.
screen: `A SINGER BY THE RIVER.` → `SONGS ABOUT HIS OWN FAILINGS.` → `A TEACHER STOPS TO LISTEN.`

segments.voice: The account comes from a book of stories about Vallabha's followers, told in Braj, the language of that country. The teacher says, roughly: why whine like this? Sing about the Lord's play, his lila. And Surdas does. He turns from his own sorrow to a child's life in a cowherd village. The songs carried under his name are called the Sursagar, the ocean of Sur, full of small household things: a cradle, a churn of yogurt, a mother calling her boy in to eat. Here's one. Little Krishna comes to Yashoda with a complaint. Mother, when will my braid grow? You keep telling me to drink my milk and it'll get long and thick like my brother Balarama's. I've drunk and drunk, and it's still short. A tiny boy comparing hair with his big brother, suspecting his mother of a trick. That's the whole song, and it is a song about God. Bhakti has a name for this kind of love: vatsalya, the tenderness of a parent for a child. Instead of looking up at God from far below, the singer stands where Yashoda stands and looks down, at someone small enough to worry about. And the singer's own failings? Nobody told him they didn't matter. He was told to look somewhere else. Tradition says he kept singing in that voice, the voice of mothers and cowherd girls, for the rest of his life.
screen: `WHY WHINE? SING HIS PLAY.` · `THE SURSAGAR: THE OCEAN OF SUR.` · `MOTHER, WHEN WILL MY BRAID GROW?` · then, large: `LOOK DOWN, LIKE A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Notice, without arguing, whatever your mind likes to sing about you: what's wrong, what's late, what isn't enough. Then turn gently, the way the teacher turned Surdas, toward someone small or in your care, a child, a parent, even an animal, and hold them the way Yashoda holds a boy with a short braid: a little worry, a lot of fondness. If you pray, let that tenderness be your prayer.
Surdas. A singer of Braj who, tradition says, was blind, and who turned from his own sorrow to sing of a child named Krishna.
Your line: look down, like a mother. The sad song about yourself can make room for someone small. Until tomorrow.

928.title: Surdas
928.hook: a small boy with butter on his face makes his case
928.howItsDone: Maiya mori, main nahin makhan khayo is sung as a bhajan in homes and temples, and around Krishna's birthday, Janmashtami, children sometimes act out the butter thief's story.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Surdas turned from his own sorrow to a little boy asking when his braid would grow. Look down, like a mother.

The complaint comes from the neighbors. Butter is missing from their houses again. Pots are cracked. There are small handprints. So the accused is brought before his mother, and the song lets us see his face, still shiny with butter. He doesn't cry or run. He opens his mouth and begins his defense. It's one of the songs carried under the name of Surdas, and it plays like a tiny courtroom: one small boy, no lawyer, and an argument he has clearly been working on.
screen: `THE NEIGHBORS COMPLAIN.` → `BUTTER ON HIS FACE.` → `THE DEFENSE BEGINS.`

segments.voice: It opens with the line the whole song hangs on. Maiya mori, main nahin makhan khayo. Mother, I didn't eat the butter. Then the case, point by point. One: at dawn you sent me off behind the cows, and I wandered the forest all day. When would I have had time? Two: look at these arms. I'm a child. How could I reach a pot hung up high? Three: the cowherd boys have it in for me. They smeared it on my face themselves. Then he changes tactics and gets hurt. Mother, you're too trusting, you believe whatever they say. Maybe you think I'm somebody else's child. And the big finish: here, take back my stick and my blanket. I quit. You've made me dance enough. The song ends: Surdas says, then Yashoda smiled, and pulled him close against her heart. Case closed. The butter never comes up again. The Bhagavata told how the butter thief stole. Surdas adds the defense, and gives the last word to a mother's smile. Her love doesn't wait for the verdict, or need him to be innocent. And the singer writes his own name into the last line, standing in the yard as a witness, watching Yashoda laugh. For a singer the tradition remembers as blind, it's a striking place to stand: the one who sees the scolding turn into a hug.
screen: `MOTHER, I DIDN'T EAT THE BUTTER.` · `DAWN, SMALL ARMS, JEALOUS FRIENDS.` · `TAKE BACK MY STICK. I QUIT.` · then, large: `YASHODA SMILED AND PULLED HIM CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who gets things wrong around you and argues their way out: a child, a coworker, maybe you. Hear the defense the way Yashoda hears it, every point lined up, a little dramatic, and instead of ruling on it, picture smiling and opening your arms. You don't have to agree with the argument; just let the warmth arrive first, and if you pray, bring that person into your prayer.
Surdas. The singer who let a small boy argue his case, and gave the last line to his mother's smile.
Your line: warmth before the verdict. A mother's smile settled the whole case. See you tomorrow.

929.title: Surdas
929.hook: a learned messenger comes to teach the gopis, and a bee gets an earful
929.carry: our one mind went with Shyam
929.howItsDone: Bhramargit songs from the Sursagar are sung in Krishna devotion, and the meeting of Uddhava and the gopis is retold in kirtan, dance and Ras Lila performances in the Braj region.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Surdas let a boy with butter on his face argue his case, and gave the last line to Yashoda's smile.

Krishna has gone. He grew up, left for the city of Mathura, and didn't come back. In Braj, the cowherd girls, the gopis, are still waiting at the edge of the village. Then a chariot comes down the road, and it isn't him. It's his friend Uddhava, a learned man, with a message. Krishna is everywhere, he tells them. Stop grieving for a body. Close your eyes, practice yoga, meditate on the one without form. He has come to teach them. He hasn't come expecting to be taught.
screen: `KRISHNA HAS GONE TO THE CITY.` → `A CHARIOT, BUT NOT HIM.` → `UDDHAVA BRINGS A LESSON.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata tells this scene, and in it one of the gopis, deep in sorrow, starts talking to a bee that has landed near her, scolding it as if it were Krishna's go-between. That little bee became a doorway. The gopis' bee songs are called the bhramargit, and in the Sursagar Surdas fills them with sharp, funny, grieving answers to Uddhava. Here's one. Udho, man na bhaye das bees. Uddhava, we don't have ten or twenty minds. We had one, and it went with Shyam. So who's left here to meditate on your formless one? It's airtight. Uddhava's method needs a mind to sit still. Theirs walked off down the road to Mathura. In other songs they needle him: you've hauled a load of yoga to a village of milkmaids; take it back to the city, nobody here is buying. And between the jokes they keep asking the bee: does he remember us? The river, the cows? Two ways toward God meet in this yard: knowledge of the formless, and love for one with a face. Surdas lets the gopis win the argument. The Bhagavata says Uddhava left wishing he could be a creeper or a bush in Braj, just to be touched by the dust of their feet. But the scene doesn't mock him. He brought the highest teaching he knew, and the tradition keeps both roads open, the path of knowing and the path of love. What Surdas adds is love heard from the inside: a heart that has given its whole mind away.
screen: `A GOPI SCOLDS A BEE.` · `WE DON'T HAVE TEN OR TWENTY MINDS.` · `OUR ONE MIND WENT WITH SHYAM.` · then, large: `UDDHAVA WISHES TO BE A CREEPER IN BRAJ.`

segments.voice: Notice how many minds came with you: the one making lists, the one replaying a conversation, the one checking the time. Don't fight them; just ask quietly, where has my one mind gone today, and let the answer be honest. Then let your attention rest where it truly is, and if you pray, turn that one mind toward God.
Surdas. The singer who gave the gopis the last word against a learned messenger: we had one mind, and it went with Shyam.
Your line: our one mind went with Shyam. Uddhava counted ten or twenty minds; the gopis had only the one. That's day nine hundred twenty-nine.

930.title: Mirabai's songs
930.hook: a cup of poison, and a woman who laughs as she drinks it
930.howItsDone: Mira bhajans are sung in homes, temples and concerts, and her life is retold in plays, films and devotional story sessions.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Surdas's gopis told a learned messenger, we had one mind, and it went with Shyam.

A cup is carried into a woman's room. Inside it, the song says, is poison, sent by the Rana, the head of the royal family she married into. She knows exactly what it is. She drinks it, and she laughs. And the poison, the song says, turned to nectar. That woman is Mirabai, and the remarkable thing is who tells the story. Not a court record. Songs sung in her voice. So who is this woman, singing about a cup of poison?
screen: `A CUP FROM THE RANA.` → `SHE DRINKS, AND LAUGHS.` → `WHO IS SINGING?`

segments.voice: What reaches us of Mira comes mostly through songs sung under her name and stories told about her, and tradition weaves the two together. Tradition says she was a Rajput princess who loved Krishna from girlhood. One story: a wandering holy man gave the child a small image of Krishna, and she wouldn't let it go. Another: watching a wedding procession, she asked her mother who her own bridegroom would be, and her mother, half joking, pointed to Krishna. Mira took her at her word. Married into the royal house of Mewar, she kept singing and dancing in the temple among wandering sadhus, and her husband's family took it as a disgrace. The songs tell of attempts to stop her: the cup of poison, and a basket said to hold a snake that, when she opened it, was a garland. Through it all she sings to Krishna as Giridhar, the one who lifted the mountain, and calls him her husband, her beloved, the one she belongs to. Now the honest part. Other singers have sung in Mira's voice too, and some readers ask which songs go back to Mira herself. What reaches us is still a clear voice. Not a saint on a pedestal. A woman who knows the poison is poison, drinks it anyway, and laughs, because she has already decided whose she is.

931.title: Mirabai's songs
931.hook: mine is Giridhar Gopal, and no one else
931.howItsDone: Mere to Giridhar Gopal is sung as a bhajan in homes, temples and concerts, often in a simple call-and-response that lets anyone join the refrain.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mirabai's songs began with a cup of poison she knew was poison. She drank, and laughed.

Some songs argue. Some plead. This one simply states a fact, the way you'd give someone your address. Mere to Giridhar Gopal, doosro na koi. Mine is Giridhar Gopal, and no one else. It's one of the songs sung in Mira's voice, short enough to carry in your pocket. And it closes a week of singers who each found a way to belong.
screen: `SOME SONGS ARGUE.` → `THIS ONE STATES A FACT.` → `MINE IS GIRIDHAR GOPAL.`

segments.voice: Mine is Giridhar Gopal, the mountain-lifter, the cowherd, and no one else. The one who wears the peacock-feather crown, he is my husband. That word, husband, is the scandal and the point. Tradition says she was married to a prince. In the song, she says plainly that she belongs to someone else. Then she counts the cost. Father, mother, brothers, relatives: she has let them go. Sitting among the holy ones, she says, I've lost lok laj, the world's sense of shame. What can anyone do to me now? Then an image that's hard to forget. With my tears, again and again, I watered the vine of love. Now it has spread, and it bears its fruit of joy. Notice the order. Not: I belong to no one, so I'm free. The reverse: I belong so completely to one that the world's opinion has lost its grip. That's a logic of bhakti, folded into one song. Now the week. Tulsidas gave Hanuman's song, a servant whose strength comes from the one he serves. Surdas stood in Yashoda's yard, turned his sorrow toward a child, gave a butter-faced boy his defense, and gave the gopis their answer: our one mind went with Shyam. And Mira says: mine is Giridhar, and no one else. Three singers, one shape. Each belongs to someone, and the belonging sets the song free.
screen: `HE IS MY HUSBAND.` · `I'VE LOST THE WORLD'S SHAME.` · `TEARS WATERED THE VINE OF LOVE.` · then, large: `THREE SINGERS, ONE SHAPE.`

segments.voice: Let the breath come and go slowly, like water poured on a young vine, and ask one plain question: whose am I? Not what do I do, but whose: a person, a community, God, a promise you keep. Let the answer come in your own words or none, notice whether some opinion out there has a little less grip on you, and if you pray, rest in the one you belong to.
Mirabai's songs. Mine is Giridhar Gopal, and no one else: belonging so complete that the world's shame lost its hold.
Your line: mine is Giridhar Gopal. Belonging came first, and the freedom followed. Day nine hundred thirty-one, done.
